## Cite these facts (do not invent others)
- Streaming loudness target in CoProducer reports: −14 LUFS integrated (pass within 1.5 LU). Apple Sound Check ≈ −16 LUFS.
- True-peak ceiling: −1.0 dBTP (Amazon Music often −2.0 dBTP).
- Release-ready score: ≥ 90 / 100. Clipped samples must be 0. Sample rate ≥ 44.1 kHz. Phase correlation ≥ 0.2.
- Auto-repair may apply loudnorm, a true-peak limiter, and a conservative 25 Hz high-pass. It does not reconstruct clipped transients or auto-fix phase.
- The website does **not** download a repaired master. It projects post-repair stats. Desktop CoProducer writes the WAV.
- Public A/B proofs (engine reports, 45 s aligned excerpts): Crazy Stacy 70→90 (831 clips→0); BeatGoHard 77→95 (true peak −0.3→−1.0 dBTP); Drippin 66→93 (231,310 clips→0, LUFS −11.92→−14.12).
- Price: free demo; Pro $49 one-time. Not a monthly subscription.

# Lacquer essays

## Parallel compression sounds thin? Check the latency first
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/parallel-compression-sounds-thin-check-latency.html
Section: Mix craft · 16 October 2026 · 8 min
Summary: Parallel compression making drums or vocals thinner? The parallel bus is probably arriving late. Find the offset, fix the timing, then dial it in.

If bringing up a parallel compressor makes the drums thinner, hollower or flammy instead of bigger, the parallel bus is usually arriving late: a few samples to a few milliseconds of uncompensated latency turns the blend into a comb filter. Null-test the two paths, measure the offset, and fix the timing before you touch the compressor.
You know the move. Drum bus feeding a parallel aux, a compressor on it slammed at 10:1 with fast attack, and you ease that fader up expecting the kit to get thick and loud. Instead the snare loses its middle, the cymbals turn a little swishy, and the kick somehow feels smaller. So you swap compressors. Then you try a different attack. Same thing.
More often than not, the compressor isn’t the problem. The parallel copy is landing a few samples after the dry one, and two copies of the same drums, slightly apart in time, don’t add up. They comb.

### What a late copy does to the blend
Add a signal to a delayed copy of itself and some frequencies arrive in phase (louder) while others arrive opposite (cancelled). The cancellations fall at regular spacing, like the teeth of a comb. With a delay of N samples at sample rate fs, the first notch sits at fs / (2·N) and they repeat every fs / N above it.
With true parallel compression the copy isn’t identical (it’s squashed), so the notches aren’t bottomless. But their depth changes as the compressor breathes, because the level ratio between the two paths keeps moving. That’s the swishy, faintly flanged thing on cymbals and room mics. It’s not your compressor’s character. It’s timing.
Where the offset lands decides what you hear:
Offset at 48 kHz | First notch | What it usually sounds like
1–4 samples | 24–6 kHz | Top end a little duller than solo; easy to blame the compressor’s tone
8–64 samples (0.2–1.3 ms) | 3 kHz–375 Hz | Hollow snare, papery vocal, “phasey” overheads
128–512 samples (2.7–10.7 ms) | 188–47 Hz | Snare body and kick weight drop out; blend stops getting louder
1,000+ samples (20 ms+) | under 25 Hz | A flam or slap: you hear two hits, not one thicker one

### We measured it on a drum loop
To put numbers on it we built a synthetic drum loop (pitched-sine kick, noise-and-tone snare, hats, a small stereo room) at 48 kHz, ran a copy through a fast 10:1 compressor (about 9.4 dB of gain reduction on hits), matched its RMS to the dry loop, and blended it in at −4 dB. Then we slid the parallel path late by different amounts and compared each blend with the perfectly aligned one. Synthetic test signals, so read the shape rather than the decimals.
Parallel late by | First notch | Kick 40–120 | Body 150–400 | Crack 1.2–4k | Air 4–16k | Blend adds | L/R correlation
0 (aligned) | — | 0.0 | 0.0 | 0.0 | 0.0 | +4.0 dB | 0.89
1 sample | 24 kHz | 0.0 | 0.0 | −0.1 | −1.9 | +3.4 dB | 0.88
8 samples (0.17 ms) | 3 kHz | 0.0 | +0.1 | −6.0 | −2.7 | +3.4 dB | 0.89
32 samples (0.67 ms) | 750 Hz | −0.1 | −0.1 | −2.6 | −2.5 | +3.3 dB | 0.89
64 samples (1.33 ms) | 375 Hz | −0.3 | −1.5 | −2.5 | −2.6 | +3.1 dB | 0.89
128 samples (2.67 ms) | 188 Hz | −1.3 | −7.1 | −2.8 | −2.6 | +2.2 dB | 0.90
512 samples (10.7 ms) | 47 Hz | −3.8 | −1.1 | −2.6 | −2.6 | +0.8 dB | 0.86
1,024 samples (21.3 ms) | 23 Hz | −1.2 | −1.5 | −2.4 | −2.6 | +2.3 dB | 0.90
Band columns are dB relative to the aligned blend. Three things in there are worth carrying into your next session.
- Even one sample costs you air. Aligned, the parallel copy adds in phase all the way up. Late by anything, it adds in phase at some frequencies and against at others, so above the first few notches it only adds power, not amplitude. That’s the 2–3 dB of top end that went missing in every misaligned row, and individual notches dug 13–16 dB deep.
- The notch walks down as the offset grows. Eight samples took 6 dB out of the snare crack. A hundred and twenty-eight took 7 dB out of the body. Half a block of latency (512 samples) cancelled the kick fundamental. Each is a different “this compressor sounds wrong” complaint with the same cause.
- The blend stops getting louder. Aligned, the parallel bus added 4.0 dB. At 512 samples it added 0.8 dB, so you push the fader further, which digs the notches deeper. That feedback loop is how a drum bus ends up with the parallel aux at +6 and still sounding small.
The last column matters too. Correlation barely moved (0.86–0.90 in every row) because both channels comb the same way. A correlation meter, CoProducer’s phase row included, will pass this mix, and that’s honest: it answers whether left and right will cancel in mono, not whether two busses inside the session line up. Different question, different test.

### Where the latency sneaks in
Modern DAWs compensate plugin latency automatically, which is why this catches good engineers. It breaks in a handful of predictable places:
- Low-latency monitoring modes. Logic’s Low Latency Mode, Ableton’s Reduced Latency When Monitoring, Cubase’s Constrain Delay Compensation and friends trade compensation for tracking feel. Leave one on after a vocal session and your parallel paths drift.
- Lookahead and oversampling on one path only. A compressor in lookahead or high-quality mode, a linear-phase EQ, or a saturator with oversampling adds anywhere from a few samples to thousands. If the plugin reports it wrong, or changes it when you flip a quality switch mid-playback, compensation can be off until you stop and restart the transport.
- Hardware inserts. An outboard compressor through spare I/O needs its round trip measured (the ping or delay-compensation setting on the insert). An unpinged insert is the classic 1–3 ms parallel smear.
- Odd routing. Aux feeding aux, sidechain-fed chains, or a send taken from a different point than the dry signal. Not every DAW compensates every path the same way.
- Printed parallels. You bounced the crushed bus in place to save CPU and the print came back shifted or trimmed. Now there’s no plugin left to blame.

### Find it in one minute: the null test
Don’t bypass anything for this. In some DAWs a bypassed plugin drops its latency, which hides exactly what you’re looking for.
1. On the parallel bus, set the compressor so it does nothing: ratio 1:1 or threshold all the way up, make-up at 0 dB.
2. Flip polarity on the parallel bus and set its fader so its level matches the dry path (unity if the send is post-fader at 0 dB).
3. Play the drums. Aligned paths null to near silence. If you still hear a thin, fizzy version of the kit, the paths are apart.
On the loop above, aligned paths nulled to −175 dB (numerical floor). One sample of offset left a residual only 3.0 dB under the dry level, on this hat-heavy loop. Sixty-four samples left −0.8 dB, and 128 made the “null” 2.2 dB louder than the dry. There’s no such thing as nearly aligned. A miss is a miss.
If you’d rather have a number than a vibe, bounce the dry drums and the parallel bus soloed, same start point, and let this work out the lag. It cross-correlates the two files and tells you which path to delay:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""find_offset.py — how late is one bounce relative to another?
Bounce the dry track (or bus) soloed and the parallel bus soloed, same start point, then:
    python3 find_offset.py dry.wav parallel.wav
Prints the lag in samples and ms, the first comb notch it implies, and how well the two line up."""
import sys, subprocess, numpy as np

def load(path):   # any format ffmpeg reads -> mono float, plus its sample rate
    sr = int(subprocess.run(["ffprobe", "-v", "error", "-select_streams", "a:0", "-show_entries", "stream=sample_rate",
                             "-of", "csv=p=0", path], capture_output=True, text=True, check=True).stdout)
    raw = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", path, "-ac", "1", "-f", "f32le", "-"], capture_output=True, check=True).stdout
    return np.frombuffer(raw, np.float32).astype(np.float64), sr

a, sr = load(sys.argv[1]); b, sr_b = load(sys.argv[2])
assert sr == sr_b, "bounce both files at the same sample rate"
n = min(len(a), len(b), sr * 30)                  # 30 s is plenty
a, b = a[:n] - a[:n].mean(), b[:n] - b[:n].mean()
size = 1 << int(np.ceil(np.log2(2 * n)))
xc = np.fft.irfft(np.fft.rfft(b, size) * np.conj(np.fft.rfft(a, size)), size)
max_lag = sr // 10                                # search +/-100 ms
lags = np.r_[np.arange(0, max_lag), np.arange(-max_lag, 0)]
vals = np.r_[xc[:max_lag], xc[-max_lag:]]
k = int(np.argmax(np.abs(vals))); lag = int(lags[k])
score = abs(vals[k]) / np.sqrt(np.sum(a ** 2) * np.sum(b ** 2))
pol = "same" if vals[k] > 0 else "FLIPPED"
print(f"{sys.argv[2]} vs {sys.argv[1]}: {lag:+d} samples ({lag / sr * 1000:+.2f} ms) at {sr} Hz")
print(f"match {score:.2f} (1.00 = identical shape), polarity {pol}")
if lag:
    print(f"blending them comb-filters: first notch ~{sr / (2 * abs(lag)):.0f} Hz, then every {sr / abs(lag):.0f} Hz")
    print(f"fix: delay the {'dry path' if lag > 0 else 'parallel path'} by {abs(lag)} samples, or fix the plugin delay compensation")
else:
    print("aligned to the sample")
On our loop, with the parallel path deliberately 64 samples late:
wet_late.wav vs dry.wav: +64 samples (+1.33 ms) at 48000 Hz
match 0.86 (1.00 = identical shape), polarity same
blending them comb-filters: first notch ~375 Hz, then every 750 Hz
fix: delay the dry path by 64 samples, or fix the plugin delay compensation
A match score under 1.00 is expected here, since one side is compressed. The lag is what you came for.

### Fix order
1. Turn compensation back on fully and restart playback. That alone fixes most of these.
2. Ping any hardware inserts.
3. If the routing can’t be compensated, put the measured offset on the dry path’s track delay (most DAWs take it in samples or ms) and run the null test again until it disappears.
4. Only now dial the compressor. You’ll probably need less of the parallel fader than before, because the blend is finally adding up.
Once it’s aligned, the genre moves behave the way the tutorials promise. Rock and pop drum busses take a fast, hard-ratio parallel tucked well under the dry and get density without losing the snare’s crack. On R&B and pop vocals, a parallel tucked a few dB under the lead thickens the low-level detail without that papery phasiness. On trap 808s with parallel saturation, alignment protects the fundamental. Remember the 512-sample row: it cost the kick 3.8 dB.
And if you want two hits, do it on purpose. A parallel slap delayed 20 ms or more is a legitimate effect. The trouble is the 0.1–10 ms zone nobody chose.
Note: Plugins with a built-in mix knob usually avoid all this, because the dry and wet signals share the same internal latency. When a mix knob sounds fuller than the same compressor on an aux, the aux is probably late. For the stereo side of phase, read Phase correlation is a mono audition. If the bus is pumping rather than thinning, the sidechain filter essay is the one you want.
Q: Why does parallel compression make my drums sound thin?
A: Usually because the parallel bus arrives a few samples to a few milliseconds after the dry signal. The two copies comb-filter, cancelling some frequencies and losing top-end coherence, so the blend gets hollower instead of bigger. Null-test the paths and fix the latency before changing compressor settings.
Q: How much delay causes phasing in parallel compression?
A: Any. On our synthetic drum loop a single sample at 48 kHz cost about 2 dB in the 4–16 kHz band, 8 samples took 6 dB out of the 1.2–4 kHz crack, and 128 samples took 7 dB out of the snare body. The first notch sits at the sample rate divided by twice the offset.
Q: Does a compressor’s mix knob avoid the latency problem?
A: Usually, yes. With a built-in dry/wet control both signals go through the same plugin latency, so they stay aligned. The problem shows up when the dry and compressed signals take different routes through the session.
Q: Will a phase correlation meter catch a misaligned parallel bus?
A: No. Both channels comb-filter the same way, so left/right correlation barely moves. Our blends read 0.86–0.90 whether aligned or 1,024 samples late. Use a polarity-flip null test or cross-correlate soloed bounces instead.

## Why your gapless album gets gaps after MP3 or AAC
URL: https://myaiplug.github.io/coproducer-web/blog/gapless-album-gaps-after-mp3-or-aac.html
Section: Delivery · 16 October 2026 · 7 min
Summary: MP3 and AAC encoders add silence at the start and padding at the end of every file. Why segues break, what we measured, and how to stay seamless.

Every MP3 and AAC encoder adds a little silence at the start of a file and pads the end out to a full frame, so two tracks that flowed perfectly as WAVs can play with a 5–30 ms hole or a tick between them unless the file carries gapless info and the player reads it. Render the album in one pass, split it at exact sample positions, deliver lossless, and count samples on anything you encode yourself.
Live record, DJ mix, ambient album, a concept project where track 4 pours into track 5 under a held chord. In the session it’s one long, beautiful sentence. Then you make MP3s for the press folder, or a client plays the AAC previews in a car, and right at the segue there’s a hiccup. A tiny hole, sometimes a tick. Nobody touched the transition. The files did.
Single-song releases don’t care about any of this. A few tens of milliseconds of silence before a single is inaudible. It only bites when one track is supposed to keep flowing into the next.

### Where the hole comes from
Lossy codecs work in frames, and the encoder needs a run-up before the first one. So every MP3 and AAC file starts with a short stretch of priming (encoder delay) and ends with padding that fills out the last frame. The file is a little longer than your audio, on both ends.
There’s a fix built into the formats, as long as everyone plays along. LAME writes the exact delay and padding into a header in the first frame (the LAME/Info tag). MP4 files use an edit list (Apple’s encoders also write an iTunSMPB tag). Opus stores a pre-skip in its header. A player that reads these trims the priming and padding and plays your audio sample for sample. A player that doesn’t plays the silence, and two of those silences back to back are your gap.

### What we measured
We rendered a synthetic 20-second segue at 44.1 kHz (a sustained pad chord, a low pulse, a little noise for air) and split it into two tracks at sample 441,123. That’s deliberately mid-note, at −12.4 dBFS, not on a zero crossing. Then we encoded both halves the common ways, decoded them back to back with ffmpeg the way a player would, and compared the join with the continuous original.
Delivery / playback | Lead-in | Extra at end | Track 2 arrives late | Dip at the join | Join null (mid-track)
24-bit WAV or FLAC, split from one render | 0 | 0 | 0 | none | −128.7 dB (−128.5)
Each track bounced separately, 10 ms edge fades | 0 | 0 | 0 | −6.0 dB | −10.2 dB (−184.6)
MP3 (LAME 320k), tag read | 0 | 0 | 0 | none | −36.7 dB (−36.5)
Same MP3, player ignores the tag | 1,105 | 140 | 28.2 ms | silence (−90 dB) | —
MP3 written without the tag | 1,105 | 140 | 28.2 ms | silence (−90 dB) | —
AAC .m4a (ffmpeg aac 256k), edit list read | 0 | 221 | 5.0 ms | −23.1 dB | −16.1 dB (−38.2)
Same .m4a, edit list ignored / raw .aac | 1,024 | 221 | 28.2 ms | −29.4 dB | −16.1 dB (−38.2)
Lead-in and extra are in samples. “Dip” is the quietest 2 ms right at the join compared with the same spot in the original. “Join null” re-aligns track 2 and nulls ±50 ms around the cut against the original, with the same measure from the middle of the track in brackets, so you can see whether the join is any worse than the codec already is.
- Lossless split from one render is perfect. The two WAVs put back together match the original to 24-bit rounding, even cut mid-note. You don’t need zero crossings when nothing is going to be re-encoded at the edges.
- A tagged MP3 is seamless, if the player reads the tag. With the tag honoured, the join nulled exactly as well as the middle of the track (−36.7 vs −36.5 dB), which means it’s only codec noise. Ignore the tag, or never write it, and you get 1,245 samples of pure digital silence: 28.2 ms, right in the middle of your held chord.
- AAC was the touchier one here. With ffmpeg’s built-in encoder the start was trimmed, but 221 samples of end padding stayed in, and the edges reconstructed noticeably worse than the middle of the file (−16 vs −38 dB). That reads as a small smeared tick rather than a clean hole. Other AAC encoders and players behave differently, which is exactly why you test the pair you’re shipping.
- You can break it before any codec gets near it. Bouncing each song as its own region with default edge fades gave a 6 dB dip at the join in a lossless WAV. No encoder will fix that.

### What’s yours to control
For streaming releases you upload WAV or FLAC and the platform does its own encoding and gapless playback. You can’t control their decoder, but you control whether the files you hand them are continuous to the sample, and that’s the part that breaks most often. If your distributor’s form asks whether the album should play continuously or gapless, say yes.
Anything you encode yourself is all on you: press MP3s, a DJ pool upload, the player on your own site, previews for a client. Use an encoder that writes gapless info (LAME does by default) and check the result.

### The workflow
1. Do the transitions in one session and render once. Crossfades, reverb tails, room tone between live songs: all of it lives in the long render. Dither once on that render if you’re going to 16-bit, then split.
2. Split at sample positions, not by bouncing regions. No auto-fades at the cut points, no per-track normalize, no tail trimming. The tracks should butt together and reassemble into the original exactly.
3. For CD, author from the continuous file. Red Book audio is addressed in frames of 1/75 s (588 samples at 44.1 kHz), and track marks in a DDP land on those frames. If a plant insists on individual WAVs, put the splits on 588-sample boundaries so the authoring tool has nothing to pad.
4. Encode with gapless metadata, then count samples. Every encoded track should decode to the same number of samples as its WAV.
Here’s steps 2 and 4 as a script. It cuts one album render at the sample positions you give it, writes 24-bit WAVs for delivery, and makes LAME-tagged MP3s for anything you hand out. The optional --cd flag snaps the splits to CD frames.
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# split_album.sh — cut one continuous album render into tracks at exact sample positions,
# write 24-bit WAVs for delivery plus gapless-tagged MP3s for anything you hand out yourself.
#   ./split_album.sh album_full.wav markers.txt [--cd]
# markers.txt: one track START per line, in samples (0 for track 1). --cd snaps starts to 588-sample CD frames.
set -euo pipefail
src=$1; markers=$2; cd_snap=${3:-}
sr=$(ffprobe -v error -select_streams a:0 -show_entries stream=sample_rate -of csv=p=0 "$src")
total=$(ffprobe -v error -select_streams a:0 -count_packets -show_entries stream=duration_ts -of csv=p=0 "$src")
mapfile -t starts < <(grep -v '^\s*$' "$markers")
[[ $cd_snap == --cd ]] && for i in "${!starts[@]}"; do starts[$i]=$(( (starts[$i] + 294) / 588 * 588 )); done
starts+=("$total")
for (( i = 0; i < ${#starts[@]} - 1; i++ )); do
  a=${starts[$i]}; b=${starts[$((i + 1))]}; n=$(printf "%02d" $((i + 1)))
  ffmpeg -v error -y -i "$src" -af "atrim=start_sample=$a:end_sample=$b,asetpts=N/SR/TB" -c:a pcm_s24le "track$n.wav"
  ffmpeg -v error -y -i "track$n.wav" -c:a libmp3lame -b:a 320k "track$n.mp3"   # LAME/Xing tag carries delay + padding
  echo "track$n  samples $a-$b  ($(( b - a )) samples, $(awk "BEGIN{printf \"%.3f\", ($b-$a)/$sr}") s)"
done
On our segue, with markers at 0 and 441123:
track01  samples 0-441123  (441123 samples, 10.003 s)
track02  samples 441123-882000  (440877 samples, 9.997 s)
Then the check. Each encoded file should decode to exactly the sample count of its WAV:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# count_samples.sh — does each encoded track decode to exactly as many samples as its WAV?
#   ./count_samples.sh track01 track02 ...   (expects trackNN.wav next to trackNN.mp3 / .m4a)
for t in "$@"; do
  wav=$(ffmpeg -v error -i "$t.wav" -f s16le -ac 1 - | wc -c)
  for enc in "$t".mp3 "$t".m4a; do
    [[ -f $enc ]] || continue
    dec=$(ffmpeg -v error -i "$enc" -f s16le -ac 1 - | wc -c)
    printf '%-14s %9d samples   wav %9d   extra %+d\n' "$enc" $((dec / 2)) $((wav / 2)) $(((dec - wav) / 2))
  done
done
From the split above (MP3 from the script, plus an ffmpeg AAC for comparison):
track01.mp3       441123 samples   wav    441123   extra +0
track01.m4a       441344 samples   wav    441123   extra +221
track02.mp3       440877 samples   wav    440877   extra +0
track02.m4a       441344 samples   wav    440877   extra +467
And the same MP3s written without the tag came back +1,245 and +1,491 samples longer. That’s the gap, measured in advance instead of discovered by a listener. +0 means the decoder knows where your audio starts and stops. Anything else is a gap waiting for a segue.
Screw tapes were continuous by design, and the rule carries over: whether the slowdowns come from ScrewAI or a turntable pass, blend the tape in one session, render it once and cut it after. Don’t bounce every song separately and hope the joins line up.
Note: Encoders change more than timing. Re-encoding eats true-peak headroom covers what they do to your peaks. And if a track’s leading silence is dragging its loudness reading down, that’s a different edge problem with its own fix.
Q: Why is there a gap between tracks on my album after converting to MP3?
A: MP3 encoders add priming silence at the start and padding at the end of every file. LAME records both in a header so players can trim them. If the tag is missing or the player ignores it, the silences play. In our test that was a 28.2 ms hole at 44.1 kHz.
Q: Do I need to split album tracks at zero crossings?
A: Not for lossless delivery. Two WAVs cut from one render reassemble exactly, even mid-note. What matters is cutting at a single sample position with no fades, trims or per-track processing at the cut.
Q: Do streaming platforms fix gapless playback for me?
A: They encode from your lossless files and handle playback themselves, so you can’t control their decoder. You do control whether the files you upload are continuous to the sample. A dip or fade baked into your WAVs survives every platform.
Q: How do I check that an MP3 or AAC file is gapless?
A: Decode it and compare its sample count with the WAV it came from. A tagged LAME MP3 decoded by ffmpeg matched exactly in our test. An untagged one was 1,245 samples longer, and an ffmpeg AAC .m4a kept 221 samples of end padding.
